sender.en: “A roofer working nearby” at your door

name.en: Rogue roofers: “your roof needs urgent repairs”

how.en: Traders knock on the door, or call after you post a job online, and say they have spotted a problem with your roof or gutters. They start with a low price, then “find” more damage once they are up there and demand much more. Work may be invented, never done or badly done, and payment may be demanded on the spot with intimidating pressure. Doorstep tactics were used in most suspected roofing scams reported to Citizens Advice.

text.en: A trader comes to your door saying they have noticed a problem with your roof.
They quote a low price to start the work today.
Once up the ladder, they say they found more damage that must be fixed now.
They demand a large payment straight away, sometimes refusing to leave.
Morning, we're working on a roof down the road and noticed a few of your tiles are loose. Could be a leak with all this rain. We can sort it today for £250 while we've got the ladders here.

en: said my roof tiles are loose
found more damage on the roof
builder demanded cash for roof repairs
paid for roof work never done
Cold callers offering roof or gutter work.
A low price that suddenly grows.
Pressure to pay now, especially in cash.
Say no to cold callers and don’t let them up on your roof.
Get quotes from traders you find yourself, for example through your council’s trusted trader scheme.
Report it to the Citizens Advice consumer helpline. If you feel threatened, call 999.

sources.title: Citizens Advice says roofing scams are leaving people thousands of pounds out of pocket

story.en: A 65-year-old woman living alone posted an ad about a dripping gutter. Two men came the same day and agreed £2,500 for “eave protection”. Then they “found” crumbling cement and stood at her door in the dark demanding money, and she ended up paying £3,500. The next day there was no sign of any work. She later got a refund through her bank.
